nodes.title: 集合、逻辑、量词与证明
nodes.definition: Mathematical statements specify objects, assumptions, and conclusions. Sets collect objects; membership, intersection, union, and complement describe relationships among them. Quantifiers distinguish a claim about every object from a claim that at least one object exists. A proof establishes a statement under stated assumptions, while a counterexample disproves a universal claim. Direct argument, contradiction, and induction are different proof structures. This language is needed before reading probability events, vector-space definitions, convergence guarantees, or optimization theorems. Numerical examples support understanding but cannot prove an unrestricted universal statement.
nodes.example: To evaluate whether every matrix of a certain shape is invertible, first state the domain and dimensions. One singular example disproves that universal claim; several invertible examples do not prove it.
nodes.role_en: High-school-to-university entry point for event notation, research assumptions, and ROB501 proof work.
nodes.latex: A\cap B=\{x:x\in A\land x\in B\},\qquad\forall x\in D,\;P(x)

notation.meaning: Sets; D is the domain of a quantified claim.

nodes.title: 计数、排列组合与二项系数
nodes.summary: 计数、排列组合与二项系数
nodes.definition: Counting determines how many outcomes satisfy a specification before probabilities are assigned. The product rule counts sequences of choices, while addition requires disjoint alternatives or a correction for overlap. Permutations retain order; combinations ignore order. Replacement and repeated objects change the count and must be specified. A binomial coefficient counts subsets of fixed size and also appears in repeated Bernoulli trials. Counting gives probabilities by a ratio only when the underlying elementary outcomes are equally likely; that assumption is part of the model.
nodes.example: Choose a subset of sensors from an available pool and distinguish it from assigning those sensors to ordered roles. State whether a sensor may be reused before applying a product, permutation, or combination formula.
nodes.role_en: Fills SI602 Units1–2 and the counting prerequisite for discrete distributions and probability spaces.

nodes.en: Span, Independence, Basis, Rank and Null Space
nodes.title: 张成、线性无关、基、秩与零空间
nodes.summary: 张成、线性无关、基、秩与零空间
nodes.definition: The span of vectors is the set of all their linear combinations. A linearly independent set has no redundant vector, and a basis is an independent set that spans a space. Matrix rank measures the dimension of its column space; its null space contains input directions mapped to zero. These definitions explain solvability, identifiability, and degrees of freedom in a linear model. A matrix can have many rows while still losing information through dependent columns. Dimension and rank are mathematical properties, not counts of neural network layers.
nodes.example: For a measurement matrix, identify an input direction in its null space. Adding that direction to a candidate state leaves the measurements unchanged, demonstrating an ambiguity that collecting more duplicate equations cannot remove.
nodes.role_en: Connects SI602 linear algebra to least squares, SVD, state identifiability, observability, and research proof language.

notation.meaning: Matrix acting on an n-dimensional input.

nodes.en: Orthogonal Projection, QR and Least Squares
nodes.title: 正交投影、QR与最小二乘
nodes.definition: Orthogonal projection finds the closest vector in a subspace under an inner-product norm. In linear least squares, the fitted observation lies in the column space of the design matrix and the residual is orthogonal to that space. QR factorization constructs an orthonormal basis and a triangular coordinate system for computing the solution without explicitly forming a matrix inverse. Rank deficiency changes uniqueness and requires an appropriate solution convention. This geometry unifies regression, fitting, and parts of state estimation; weighted observations require the corresponding weighted inner product.
nodes.example: Fit an overdetermined measurement system and plot the residual. Check that it is orthogonal to each design-matrix column. Compare a QR solve with explicitly inverting normal equations when the columns are nearly dependent.
nodes.role_en: Fills the mathematical mechanism between matrix multiplication and regression/estimation in ROB501, Math51, and EE263.
nodes.latex: A=QR,\quad Q^\top Q=I,\quad R\hat x=Q^\top b,\quad A^\top(b-A\hat x)=0

notation.meaning: Full-column-rank design matrix and observed vector in this reduced-QR schematic.
Orthonormal columns and invertible upper-triangular factor.
Least-squares parameter estimate.

nodes.title: 极限、收敛与不动点迭代
nodes.summary: 极限、收敛与不动点迭代
nodes.definition: A sequence converges when its terms eventually remain arbitrarily close to a limiting value in a specified metric. An iterative algorithm therefore needs a stated notion of error and assumptions that make progress imply convergence. A contraction reduces distances by a uniform factor below one; on an appropriate complete invariant domain, fixed-point theory supplies existence, uniqueness, and convergence guarantees. These conditions are stronger than observing a decreasing error for several steps. Newton-type updates can be fast locally but require additional smoothness and initialization assumptions.
nodes.example: Compare repeated application of a distance-contracting map with an update that decreases error only near its solution. Plot several initializations and distinguish numerical evidence from a convergence guarantee that explicitly states its domain and assumptions.
nodes.role_en: Provides ROB501 analysis language and a bridge from computational updates to convergence claims in optimization, solvers, and filtering.

notation.meaning: Self-map on the declared complete invariant domain.
Uniform contraction constant.
Iterate; the fixed point satisfies T(x*)=x*.

nodes.title: 凸性与Jensen不等式
nodes.definition: A convex function lies below the line segment connecting any two points in its domain, provided the domain is convex. Jensen’s inequality extends this relation from finite weighted combinations to expectations under the required integrability assumptions. It explains why applying a nonlinear function before averaging generally differs from applying it to the average. Convexity also supports optimization guarantees, but the objective and feasible set must both be examined. A neural network loss as a function of all weights is generally not made convex merely by using a familiar convex per-example error.
nodes.example: Compare the average squared error with the square of the average signed error on a small distribution. Then identify which quantity Jensen bounds and state the convex function being applied instead of memorizing an inequality direction.
nodes.role_en: Fills the CSE598 preparation link among expectation, nonlinear functions, log objectives, and convex optimization.

nodes.en: Joint Distributions, Densities, CDFs and Marginals
nodes.title: 联合分布、密度、分布函数与边缘化
nodes.summary: 联合分布、密度、分布函数与边缘化
nodes.definition: A distribution assigns probabilities to events. For continuous variables, a density must be integrated over a region; its value at a point is not a point probability. A cumulative distribution function gives the probability that a variable is below a threshold. Joint distributions describe several variables together, while marginalization removes variables by summation or integration. Conditioning renormalizes the remaining possibilities when defined. These operations distinguish correlated variables from independent ones and provide the mathematical interface used by Gaussian models, latent-variable methods, and Bayesian state estimation.
nodes.example: Given a joint density for position and measurement error, integrate out the error to obtain the position marginal. Compare a rectangular event probability with a conditional distribution and explicitly identify the normalization denominator.
nodes.role_en: Connects calculus to continuous probability, CSE598 Gaussian preparation, mixture models, latent variables, and filtering.

notation.meaning: Cumulative distribution and marginal density.

nodes.en: Estimation, Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests
nodes.title: 统计估计、置信区间与假设检验
nodes.summary: 统计估计、置信区间与假设检验
nodes.definition: Statistical inference uses finite observations to estimate population quantities or evaluate a stated hypothesis under a sampling model. An estimator is a random function of data before the sample is observed. A frequentist confidence procedure has a repeated-sampling coverage property; it is not automatically a posterior probability for one fixed realized parameter. A p-value measures the extremeness of data under a null model and test statistic, not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Effect size, assumptions, dependence, and multiple comparisons matter alongside significance.
nodes.example: Estimate a robot’s success probability from independent trials and report an interval with its sampling assumptions. If comparing controllers, specify the pairing and null hypothesis, and report the performance difference rather than only whether a significance threshold was crossed.
nodes.role_en: Adds the SI602 significance/confidence link and supports honest algorithm evaluation without reproducing any private assessment.

notation.meaning: Confidence-set procedure; coverage is a sampling property.
Chosen error level.

nodes.title: 条件数、残差与数值稳定性
nodes.summary: 条件数、残差与数值稳定性
nodes.definition: Conditioning describes how strongly an exact problem’s solution changes when its input changes. Numerical stability instead describes how an algorithm propagates rounding and approximation errors. A small residual does not necessarily imply a small solution error when the problem is ill-conditioned. Matrix singular values make this sensitivity visible, and scaling, regularization, or a different formulation can help. Solving a linear system is usually preferable to explicitly forming an inverse. These distinctions matter in least squares, robot Jacobians, covariance updates, and differentiable optimization.

nodes.title: 复数与复指数
nodes.definition: A complex number has real and imaginary components and can also be represented by magnitude and phase. Multiplication combines scaling with rotation in the complex plane. Euler’s formula connects complex exponentials to sine and cosine, providing a compact way to express periodic signals and solutions of linear systems. Complex eigenvalues of a real dynamical matrix can describe oscillation without implying that a physical sensor measures an imaginary quantity. Complex arithmetic is a prerequisite for later spectral and frequency-domain methods, not a claim that every robot policy needs complex-valued neural weights.
nodes.example: Represent a sinusoidal signal using a complex exponential, then take the real part to recover the measured signal. Relate multiplication by a unit-magnitude complex number to a planar rotation while keeping physical units and phase conventions explicit.
nodes.role_en: Provides the assumed complex-number background in ROB501 and the signals/dynamics bridge in Berkeley EECS16 and Stanford EE363.
